subtitle: RSI is the most-used indicator in trading and the most-misused. "Overbought" doesn't mean "sell". "Oversold" doesn't mean "buy". The real signals are regime classification, failure swings, and divergences — and they take this far beyond the basic 30/70 rules.

blocks.content:
RSI (Relative Strength Index) is on nearly every retail trader's chart. Most use it wrong. They short whenever RSI hits 70 and long whenever RSI hits 30. In a strong trend, that loses money for months.

This lesson covers RSI the way professional traders use it: as a regime classifier, failure swing detector, and divergence indicator. The 30/70 "overbought/oversold" framing is the beginner version. The framework here is the actual usable version.

RSI is a momentum oscillator. It measures the ratio of recent gains vs recent losses over a lookback period (default 14 candles). The output is a number from 0 to 100:

  • RSI = 50 → gains and losses balanced
  • RSI > 50 → recent gains dominate (momentum bullish)
  • RSI < 50 → recent losses dominate (momentum bearish)
  • RSI > 70 → strong recent gains (commonly called "overbought")
  • RSI < 30 → strong recent losses (commonly called "oversold")

The mistake: assuming overbought = sell signal and oversold = buy signal. In a strong uptrend, RSI can stay above 70 for WEEKS. Shorting every time it touches 70 = bleeding to death while the trend runs.

blocks.title: The regime concept
blocks.content:
RSI behaves differently in different market regimes. The first job before using RSI for any signal is to classify the regime:

  • Bullish regime: RSI averaging above 50, often touching 70-80. Bullish range is roughly 40-80. RSI of 40 is the "oversold" of this regime, not 30.
  • Bearish regime: RSI averaging below 50, often touching 20-30. Bearish range is roughly 20-60. RSI of 60 is the "overbought" of this regime, not 70.
  • Ranging regime: RSI oscillates 30-70 with regular reaches to both ends. Here the classic 30/70 levels work as mean reversion signals.

Same RSI value means different things in different regimes. Always classify first.

rows: Major dip — reversal signal in bullish regime.

blocks.content: Failure swings — the most reliable RSI reversal signal
A failure swing is when RSI reaches an overbought (70+) or oversold (30-) level, retreats, then FAILS to make a new extreme on the next push. This often signals exhaustion of the move.

rows: RSI hits >70, drops below 70, rises again but FAILS to reach the previous high (lower high on RSI)
Reversal signal — momentum exhaustion at the top
RSI hits <30, rises above 30, drops again but FAILS to reach the previous low (higher low on RSI)
Reversal signal — selling exhausted at the bottom

blocks.title: Why failure swings work
blocks.content:
A failure swing means the momentum that drove the original extreme can't be reproduced. Sellers in an uptrend (or buyers in a downtrend) are exhausted. The next move often reverses.

This is more reliable than 'RSI hit 70 so short' because failure swings have BUILT-IN confirmation — the second attempt confirms the exhaustion. Single touches of 70 are noise; failure swings are signal.
Divergences — the second most powerful RSI signal
Divergence is when PRICE and RSI move in opposite directions. The disagreement signals that the price move isn't backed by underlying momentum.

rows: Higher low (RSI making higher lows while price makes lower lows)
Trend continuation up — buying momentum still strong
Trend continuation down — selling momentum still strong

blocks.content: Most traders focus on regular divergences (reversal). Hidden divergences are often more reliable because they trade WITH the trend (continuation) — they catch healthy pullbacks rather than trying to call tops/bottoms.

blocks.title: Divergence doesn't predict timing
blocks.content:
Divergences signal that something is OFF. They don't tell you when the reversal happens. RSI can show divergence for weeks while price continues in the original direction.

Treat divergences as WARNINGS that confirm OTHER signals — not standalone entry triggers. "Divergence + key resistance + bearish reversal candle" = strong setup. Divergence alone = wait for confirmation.
RSI in chop vs RSI in trend

The same RSI movement means completely different things based on whether the market is trending or ranging:

  • Trending market: trade pullbacks to RSI ~40-50 (in uptrend) or RSI ~50-60 (in downtrend). Failure swings at extremes warn of trend exhaustion. Divergences are warnings, not entries.
  • Ranging market: trade mean reversion. RSI hits 30 → long. RSI hits 70 → short. Classic textbook usage. Works in ranges, fails in trends.

Always classify regime BEFORE applying RSI signals. Skipping this step is the most common RSI mistake.

BTC 4H chart over 2 weeks. RSI has been averaging 55-75 (bullish regime confirmed). Last 3 swing highs in price: $63K, $65K, $66K (HH). Corresponding RSI peaks: 75, 73, 68 (LOWER HIGHS — divergence!).

Concurrently, price now stalling at $66K resistance. Bearish engulfing candle just printed on 4H with above-average volume.

Three signals stacking:

  1. Regular bearish divergence on RSI (lower highs while price made higher highs)
  2. Price at confirmed resistance ($66K)
  3. Bearish engulfing pattern + volume

Trade analysis: divergence is the warning. The engulfing + resistance is the confirmation. Entry signal is the candle, not the divergence alone.

  • Entry: Limit SHORT at $65,700 (just below engulfing close)
  • SL: $66,500 (above the engulfing high)
  • TP1: $63,500 (recent swing high, now support)
  • TP2: $61,000 (next major support)

This works because divergence + level + pattern + volume = four independent signals aligned.

blocks.title: Take this with you
blocks.content:
Four rules:

  1. Classify regime FIRST. Bullish, bearish, ranging — determines which RSI signals matter.
  2. Failure swings > single touches. The exhaustion confirmation is what makes the signal.
  3. Divergences are warnings, not entries. Need confirmation from price action.
  4. Trade with the regime. Bullish regime + RSI 40 = long zone. Bearish regime + RSI 60 = short zone.

Forget the textbook 30/70 = buy/sell unless you're CERTAIN you're in a ranging market. In trends, use regime-aware levels.
